note: Start-here teaching shown before a skill's lesson: the basic ideas the lesson relies on but never introduces. Found by walking every maths topic in learning order as a learner of its class (2026-11-23: 345 skills read, 148 gaps), each entry checked by a second independent reader. See packages/learning/src/foundations.ts.

entries.concept: x² and xy: letters multiplied together
entries.evidence: The lessons use 7x² − 8xy − 4y − 4 and say 'x² and x are also unlike terms' without saying what x² or xy means.

screens.title: What x² and xy mean
text: A square tile with side 3 has area 3 × 3. We write this as 3², read '3 squared'.
In the same way x² means x × x. It does not mean x × 2.
Two letters written side by side are multiplied: xy means x × y. And 7x² means 7 × x × x.
x and x² are different amounts, so they are not like terms. If x is 3, then x is 3 but x² is 9.

check.question: If x = 5, what is x²?

entries.concept: minor, cofactor and adjoint of a 3 × 3 matrix
entries.evidence: The order-3 lesson says 'each entry of a row times its cofactor (its minor with the sign + − + …)' and the inverse lesson asks for 'all nine cofactors', but a minor is never defined.

screens.title: Minors and cofactors
text: Pick one entry of a 3 × 3 matrix. Cross out its whole row and its whole column. Four numbers remain, forming a 2 × 2 block. The determinant of that block is the minor of the entry.
The cofactor is the minor with a sign attached. The signs follow a chessboard pattern: first row + − +, second row − + −, third row + − +. A minus position flips the sign of the minor.
The determinant of the 3 × 3 matrix is: each entry of the first row times its own cofactor, all added up.
The adjoint, adj A, is the matrix of all nine cofactors with its rows written as columns.

check.question: Which sign goes with the entry in row 1, column 2?

entries.concept: what factorising means
entries.evidence: The first lesson goes straight to 'Factorise: x² − 7x + 12 = (x − 4)(x + □)' and only a later lesson mentions that factorising undoes expanding.

screens.title: Factorising is expanding backwards
text: 12 can be written as 3 × 4. The numbers 3 and 4 are factors of 12: things that multiply to make it.
An expression can also be written as things multiplied together. Doing this is called factorising, and each bracket is a factor.
You already know how to expand: (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 5x + 6. Factorising goes the other way: it starts from x² + 5x + 6 and finds the brackets (x + 2)(x + 3).
Look at where 5 and 6 came from: 2 + 3 = 5 and 2 × 3 = 6. That is the clue the lesson uses.
example: Find two numbers that multiply to 10 and add to 7: 2 and 5.

check.question: (x + 1)(x + 4) expands to x² + 5x + 4. So what does x² + 5x + 4 factorise to?

entries.concept: what a function is, the notation f(x), domain and range
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts with '(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x))' and 'f(x) = −x + 6', and a later one uses 'domain', but no earlier lesson says what a function or f(x) is.

screens.title: A function is a rule machine
text: Think of a machine: you drop a number in, it follows a fixed rule, and one number comes out. A function is such a rule. The same input always gives the same single output.
We give the machine a name, often f. Then f(x) is read 'f of x' and means the output when the input is x. It does not mean f times x.
f(x) = 2x + 1 says: double the input, then add 1. To find f(3), put 3 wherever x stands.
Two functions are usually called f and g so that we can tell them apart.

check.question: f(x) = x + 5. What is f(2)?

screens.title: Domain and range: what goes in, what comes out
text: Not every number can go into every machine. The rule 1/x cannot take 0, because dividing by 0 has no meaning.
The domain of a function is the set of inputs it is allowed to take. The range is the set of outputs that actually come out.
The notation f : A → B means the inputs come from the set A and the outputs land in the set B. The set B is called the codomain. The range is the part of B that is really reached.

check.question: Can 0 be in the domain of f(x) = 1/x?

entries.concept: opening a bracket and collecting like terms
entries.evidence: The 'think of a number' lesson says 'Expand the brackets and collect like terms' for 5(3n + 3) − 15, but no earlier lesson teaches either step.

screens.title: A number outside a bracket
text: Two lunch boxes each hold 3 idlis and 1 vada. Together that is 2 lots of 3 idlis and 2 lots of 1 vada.
A number written just outside a bracket multiplies everything inside it. This is called opening (or expanding) the bracket.
2(n + 3) means 2 × n and 2 × 3. So 2(n + 3) = 2n + 6.

check.question: Open the bracket: 3(n + 2).

screens.title: Putting like things together
text: 3 bags of marbles and 2 more bags of the same kind make 5 bags. If each bag holds n marbles, 3n + 2n = 5n.
Terms with the same letter are called like terms. You add or take away the numbers in front of them.
Plain numbers are collected with plain numbers. A term with n and a plain number cannot be joined: 5n + 6 stays as it is.

check.question: What is 4n + 3n?

entries.concept: sequence, term, and the labels aₙ and Sₙ
entries.evidence: The first lesson writes aₙ = a × r^(n − 1) and later Sₙ, but no earlier lesson explains what a term is or what the small n written low means.

screens.title: Terms and their labels
text: 3, 6, 12, 24, … is a list of numbers in a fixed order. Such a list is called a sequence, and each number in it is a term.

To point at a term we use its place. a₁ is the 1st term, a₂ is the 2nd term, and aₙ is the term in place n. The small low number is only a label for the place. It is not a power and nothing is multiplied by it.
The first term is often written simply as a.
Sₙ means the sum of the first n terms added together.

check.question: In the sequence 5, 10, 20, 40, … what is a₂?

entries.concept: the bars in |r| (size of a number without its sign)
entries.evidence: The sum-to-infinity lesson says 'When |r| < 1 the terms shrink towards 0' but the bars are not explained until a class 11 skill.

screens.title: |r| is the size of r
text: On a number line, 3 and −3 are on opposite sides of 0, but both are 3 steps away from it.
|r| means the distance of r from 0. It is the number without its sign, so it is never negative: |3| = 3 and |−3| = 3.
|r| < 1 means r is less than 1 step from 0, so r lies between −1 and 1. For example 1/2, −1/2 and −2/3 all have |r| < 1.
This matters because multiplying again and again by such a number makes things smaller each time: 8, 4, 2, 1, 1/2, … With r = 2 or r = −2 the terms would grow instead.

entries.concept: an inequality in x and y as a region; constraints and the feasible region
entries.evidence: The only lesson begins 'Each constraint ≤ is a half-plane bounded by a line; the corner points of the feasible region…' without explaining constraint, half-plane or feasible region.

screens.title: An inequality in x and y shades a region
text: The equation x + y = 4 is a straight line on the graph: (4, 0), (2, 2), (0, 4) and so on.
The inequality x + y ≤ 4 is true for far more points: every point on that line, and every point on one side of it. This half of the plane is called a half-plane, and the line is its boundary.
To find which side, test one easy point, usually (0, 0). Here 0 + 0 = 0 and 0 ≤ 4 is true, so the side containing the origin is the one we want.
example: (4, 0): 4 + 0 = 4, and 4 ≤ 4. On the boundary, so inside.

check.question: Is the point (1, 1) in the region x + y ≤ 4?

screens.title: Constraints and the feasible region
text: A constraint is a condition that must be obeyed. A problem usually has several at once.
The feasible region is the set of points that obey every constraint together: the overlap of all the half-planes. x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 keep us to the right of the y-axis and above the x-axis.
The region has straight edges. Its corner points are where two boundary lines cross, and you find one by solving those two lines as a pair of equations.
example: Constraints: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 4, x ≤ 3.
The lines x = 3 and x + y = 4 cross where 3 + y = 4, so y = 1.
(3, 1) is the one corner that is not on an axis.

check.question: Does (2, 1) obey all of x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 4 and x ≤ 3?

entries.concept: what an inequation is; the signs < > ≤ ≥; natural numbers, whole numbers, integers
entries.evidence: The first lesson begins 'An inequation has many solutions. When x must be a whole number, natural number or integer, the solution set is…' without saying what an inequation is or which numbers those names mean.

screens.title: Sentences with 'less than' and 'at most'
text: A lift says: at most 8 people. So the number of people can be 8, or 7, or fewer. Many answers are allowed, not just one.
Four signs say this in maths. < means 'is less than'. > means 'is greater than'. ≤ means 'is less than or equal to'. ≥ means 'is greater than or equal to'.
An inequation is like an equation, but with one of these signs in place of =. Every number that makes it true is a solution, and all the solutions together are called the solution set.

check.question: Is 5 ≤ 5 true?
check.answer: Yes. ≤ allows 'equal to' as well as 'less than'.

screens.title: Which numbers is x allowed to be?
text: The answer to an inequation depends on which numbers you may use. Three families have names.
Natural numbers are the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, … Whole numbers are the natural numbers and 0: 0, 1, 2, 3, …
Integers are the whole numbers and their negatives: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, … On a number line they are the evenly spaced dots on both sides of 0.
example: If x is a natural number: 1, 2.
If x is a whole number: 0, 1, 2.
If x is an integer from −5 to 5: −5, −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

check.question: Is 0 a natural number or a whole number?
check.answer: A whole number. The natural numbers start at 1.

entries.concept: what a linear programming problem is: the objective Z and 'subject to'
entries.evidence: The first lesson begins 'A linear objective takes its greatest and least values … at corner points' without saying what an objective is or what the problem is asking.

screens.title: The best choice under limits
text: A baker makes x cakes and y loaves a day. Flour and oven time are limited, so x and y cannot be anything: they must obey some inequalities. These are the constraints, and the points (x, y) that obey all of them form the feasible region.
The baker wants the most profit. If a cake earns ₹3 and a loaf ₹2, the profit is Z = 3x + 2y. The quantity to be made as large (or as small) as possible is called the objective.
A linear programming problem says: maximise (or minimise) Z subject to the constraints. 'Subject to' means 'while obeying'.
Because Z and the constraints are all straight-line expressions, the best value is found at a corner of the region, so you only need to test the corners.
example: Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

check.question: What is Z = 3x + 2y at the point (1, 1)?

entries.concept: what a logarithm is, and what 'log' with no base means
entries.evidence: The first lesson opens with the three laws 'log(xy) = log x + log y …' and 'log 2 = a' without ever saying what a logarithm is.

screens.title: A logarithm is a power
text: Start with 2 and keep multiplying by 2: 2, 4, 8. It takes three 2s multiplied together to make 8, because 2³ = 8.
A logarithm asks exactly this question: 'what power of this number gives that number?' We write log₂ 8 = 3 and read it 'log of 8 to base 2 is 3'.
The small number is called the base. In general, log of X to base B is the power y for which B raised to y equals X.
So a logarithm is not a new kind of number. It is just a power, found backwards.
example: log₂ 2 = 1, because 2 to the power 1 is 2.

check.question: What is log₁₀ 100?

screens.title: Plain 'log' means base 10, and why logs add
text: When no base is written, as in log 2 or log 3, the base is 10. So log 10 = 1, log 100 = 2 and log 1 = 0 (because 10 to the power 0 is 1).
log 2 is the power of 10 that gives 2. It is not a whole number (about 0.301), so the lesson just calls it a.
When you multiply powers of 10, the powers add: 10² × 10³ = 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10, which is 10 to the power 5. Logs are those powers, so the log of a product is the sum of the logs.
This is why logarithms were invented: they turn multiplying into adding.
example: That is the law log(xy) = log x + log y.

check.question: log 100 + log 10 equals the log of which number?

entries.concept: what a matrix is (rows, columns, entries) and why rows multiply columns
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts 'Entry (i, j) of AB combines row i of A with column j of B' with A = [[5, −2], [2, 5]], before any lesson says what a matrix is.

screens.title: A matrix is a table of numbers
text: Two shops record a day's sales. Shop 1 sold 5 pens and 2 notebooks. Shop 2 sold 3 pens and 4 notebooks. Written as a table, that is two rows of two numbers.
Take away the labels and keep only the block of numbers: that block is a matrix. Each number in it is called an entry.
Rows go across and columns go down. A matrix with 2 rows and 2 columns has order 2 × 2: rows are always said first.
This app writes a matrix one row at a time: [[5, 2], [3, 4]] has first row 5, 2 and second row 3, 4. A matrix gets a capital letter as its name, such as A.
example: The entry in row 2, column 1 is 3.

check.question: How many rows does [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] have?

screens.title: Why a row meets a column
text: A pen costs ₹10 and a notebook costs ₹30. Shop 1 sold 5 pens and 2 notebooks, so it took 5 × 10 + 2 × 30 = 110 rupees.
That is a row of quantities (5, 2) times a column of prices (10, 30): multiply the matching entries and add.

Multiplying matrices does exactly this again and again: each row of the first matrix is combined with each column of the second. The result for row i and column j is written in row i, column j of the answer.
example: The answer is the column [[110], [150]]: each shop's takings.

check.question: Combine the row (1, 2) with the column (3, 4).

entries.concept: the identity matrix I, the inverse A⁻¹ and the determinant |A| of a 2 × 2 matrix
entries.evidence: The orthogonal-matrix and message-coding lessons use AAᵀ = I and A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A, but identity, inverse, determinant and adjoint are not taught before this skill.

screens.title: The matrix that changes nothing, and the undo matrix
text: Multiplying a number by 1 leaves it unchanged. The matrix that does the same job is I = [[1, 0], [0, 1]], called the identity matrix: A × I = A.
For numbers, 5 × 1/5 = 1: multiplying by 1/5 undoes multiplying by 5. For a matrix A, the matrix that undoes it is called its inverse and is written A⁻¹. It satisfies A × A⁻¹ = I.
So if a message was changed by multiplying by A, multiplying by A⁻¹ brings it back.

check.question: What is A × I?

screens.title: Finding the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
text: For A = [[a, b], [c, d]], first work out one number: ad − bc. It is called the determinant of A and is written |A|.
Next write the adjoint, adj A = [[d, −b], [−c, a]]: swap a and d, and change the signs of b and c.
Then A⁻¹ = adj A divided by |A|: every entry is divided. If |A| = 0 you cannot divide, and A has no inverse.
example: The message is (1, 5). Numbering the alphabet 1 for A, 2 for B, 3 for C and so on, these are the letters A and E.

check.question: What is the determinant of [[2, 1], [1, 1]]?

entries.concept: writing a system of equations as AX = B
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'A system AX = B with |A| ≠ 0 has exactly one solution, X = A⁻¹B' without showing how equations become the matrices A, X and B.

screens.title: Packing equations into AX = B
text: Take the pair 2x + y = 5 and x + 3y = 10. Three things are in it: the coefficients, the unknowns, and the numbers on the right.
Put the coefficients in a matrix A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]], one row per equation. Put the unknowns in a column X = [[x], [y]] and the right sides in a column B = [[5], [10]].
Multiply A by X, row by column: row 1 gives 2x + y and row 2 gives x + 3y. So the single line AX = B says both equations at once. If a variable is missing from an equation, its coefficient is 0.
The number equation 3x = 6 is solved by dividing by 3. In the same way AX = B is solved by X = A⁻¹B, which works whenever |A| is not 0.

check.question: In the equation 2y + 2z = 6, what is the coefficient of x that goes into A?

entries.concept: remainder (what is left over)
entries.evidence: The 'Casting out nines' lesson says the digit sum 'leaves its remainder when divided by 9', but no earlier lesson says what a remainder is.

screens.title: What is left over
text: You have 11 marbles and a box that holds 9. Fill the box. Some marbles do not fit.
9 marbles go in the box. 2 marbles are left over.
The marbles left over are called the remainder. So when 11 is put into groups of 9, the remainder is 2.
If nothing is left over, the remainder is 0.
example: One box is full: that uses 9.

check.question: You have 10 marbles and a box that holds 9. How many are left over?

entries.concept: what partial fractions are and why we want them
entries.evidence: The first lesson opens with '(px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b) means…' without saying what splitting a fraction is or what it is for.

screens.title: Adding fractions, run backwards
text: You know how to add 1/2 + 1/3: over the common denominator 6 it is 5/6. Now go backwards: 5/6 can be split into the simpler pieces 1/2 and 1/3.
The same works with x. Adding 1/(x − 1) + 1/(x + 1) over the common denominator (x − 1)(x + 1) gives 2x/((x − 1)(x + 1)).
Partial fractions is the backward journey: start with one fraction whose denominator factorises, and split it into simple fractions, one for each factor. The unknown tops are called A and B.
We do this because the simple pieces are much easier to work with later, for example when integrating.

check.question: Which single fraction do the pieces 1/2 and 1/3 add up to?

entries.concept: the letter n for 'any place' in a pattern
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'the n-th number is n − 1 jumps after it' but no earlier lesson says what the letter n stands for.

screens.title: n means any place you like
text: Children stand in a line: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th. Each has a place number.
Sometimes we want to talk about any place at all, without choosing one. Then we write the letter n instead of a number.
'The n-th number' means the number in place n. If n is 5, it is the 5th number. If n is 9, it is the 9th number.
n − 1 means one less than the place number. If n is 5, then n − 1 is 4.
example: The number in place n is n × 2.
n = 10 gives 20, so the 10th number is 20.

check.question: If n is 7, what is n − 1?

entries.concept: the factorial sign n!
entries.evidence: The permutations lesson writes ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)! several lessons before the factorial sign is explained.

screens.title: What the ! sign means
text: Three friends stand in a row for a photo. The first place can be filled in 3 ways, the next in 2 ways, and the last in 1 way: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 rows.
Products like this, counting down to 1, come up so often that they have a short sign. n! is read 'n factorial' and means n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1.
So 3! = 6, 4! = 24 and 5! = 120. Also 1! = 1, and by agreement 0! = 1.
A big factorial contains the smaller ones: 5! = 5 × 4 × 3!. That is why factorials cancel so neatly in fractions.

check.question: What is 3!?

entries.concept: the name p(x), the value p(2), and quotient and remainder for polynomials
entries.evidence: The lesson on dividing a cubic writes 'p(x) = (x − r) × quotient + remainder' before any lesson says what p(x) means or what dividing one polynomial by another gives.

screens.title: p(x) is a name, p(2) is a value
text: Writing a long expression again and again is slow, so we give it a short name. p(x) is read 'p of x'. It names an expression that has x in it.
p(x) does not mean p times x.
p(2) means: put 2 in place of every x and work it out. The answer is called the value of p(x) at x = 2.

check.question: p(x) = 2x + 1. What is p(3)?

screens.title: Dividing leaves a quotient and a remainder
text: Divide 17 by 5: 5 goes 3 times and 2 is left over. We can write 17 = 5 × 3 + 2. Here 3 is the quotient and 2 is the remainder.
Polynomials divide in the same way. Dividing p(x) by x − r gives a quotient (another polynomial) and a remainder (a number), with p(x) = (x − r) × quotient + remainder.
You can always check a division by multiplying back and adding the remainder.
example: The quotient is x + 2 and the remainder is 3.

check.question: In 17 = 5 × 3 + 2, which number is the remainder?

entries.concept: the number i, complex numbers a + bi, conjugates and the set ℂ
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'The quadratic formula works over ℂ … √(b² − 4ac) = i√(4ac − b²) … a conjugate pair' without introducing i, ℂ or conjugates.

screens.title: A new number: i
text: The square of any real number is 0 or positive: 3 × 3 = 9 and (−3) × (−3) = 9. So no real number has square −1, and x² = −1 has no real solution.
Mathematicians add one new number to fix this. It is called i, and its defining property is i² = −1.
With i, every negative number gets a square root. (3i)² = 9 × i² = −9, so √(−9) = 3i. In general, for a positive number k, √(−k) = i√k.
example: √(−31) = i√31, which the lesson writes as √31i.

check.question: What is √(−16)?

screens.title: Complex numbers and conjugate pairs
text: A number of the form a + bi, with a and b real, is called a complex number. a is its real part and b is its imaginary part. The set of all complex numbers is written ℂ.
Changing the sign of the i part gives the conjugate: the conjugate of a + bi is a − bi. Together they are a conjugate pair.
A conjugate pair has a real sum and a real product: the sum is 2a and the product is a² + b², because (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² − b² × i² = a² + b².
The ± in the quadratic formula produces exactly such a pair when the discriminant is negative.
example: Sum = −2, product = 1 + 4 = 5: they match −b/a and c/a.

check.question: What is the conjugate of 4 + 7i?

entries.concept: a quadratic equation, its a, b, c, and the quadratic formula behind b² − 4ac
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'For ax² + bx + c = 0, work out the discriminant b² − 4ac', but no lesson states the quadratic formula that this comes from (the quadratics skill teaches only factorising, yet asks formula questions).

screens.title: A quadratic equation and its a, b and c
text: An equation in which the highest power of x is x² is called a quadratic equation. Every one can be arranged as ax² + bx + c = 0. This is called the standard form.
a is the number in front of x², b is the number in front of x, and c is the number on its own. Each keeps its sign. If a term is missing, its number is 0.
A solution (also called a root) is a value of x that makes the equation true.
example: Try x = 2: 4 − 10 + 6 = 0. True, so 2 is a root.
Try x = 3: 9 − 15 + 6 = 0. True, so 3 is a root.
Try x = 1: 1 − 5 + 6 = 2. Not 0, so 1 is not a root.

check.question: In 3x² + 4x − 7 = 0, what is c?

screens.title: The formula, and why b² − 4ac decides
text: There is one formula that solves every quadratic equation: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ (2a). The sign ± means do it twice, once with + and once with −.
The number under the square root, b² − 4ac, is called the discriminant.

If it is positive, the + and the − give two different answers. If it is 0, adding or taking away 0 changes nothing, so there is one answer. If it is negative, it has no real square root, so there is no real answer.
So you can count the solutions from b² − 4ac alone, before solving.
example: The discriminant was positive, and there are two solutions.

check.question: If b² − 4ac = 0, how many different solutions are there?

entries.concept: what a relation is, in everyday terms
entries.evidence: The first lesson defines a relation only as 'any subset of A × B', with nothing to say what a relation is for.

screens.title: A relation is a list of who goes with whom
text: 'Is the sister of', 'lives in', 'is less than': each of these links some things to other things. Maths calls such a link a relation.
To record one link we write an ordered pair (a, b), meaning 'a is related to b'. The order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different pairs.
A relation from A to B is then just the set of all the pairs that are linked, with the first entry from A and the second from B.
A × B is the set of every possible pair. A relation picks out some of them, which is why it is called a subset of A × B.
example: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3}. The link is 'a is less than b'.
2 is less than 3: pair (2, 3). 3 is less than nothing in B.

check.question: In the example, is (3, 2) in R?
check.answer: No, because 3 is not less than 2.

entries.concept: what a set is: elements, { }, ∈, the universal set U and n(A)
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts with 'A ∪ B collects every element in A or in B' and uses U, ∈ and n(A), but no lesson says what a set or an element is.

screens.title: A set is a clear collection
text: Think of the list of players in your class cricket team. For any child you can say for sure: in the team, or not in the team.
A set is a collection like that: for every thing, it is clear whether it belongs or not. The things in a set are called its elements.
We write a set by listing its elements inside curly brackets, with commas: A = {2, 4, 6}. Each element is written once, and the order does not matter.
The sign ∈ means 'is an element of'. So 4 ∈ A says 4 belongs to A. The number 5 does not belong to A.
example: V is the set of vowels: V = {a, e, i, o, u}.
e ∈ V, because e is in the list.
b is not an element of V.

check.question: A = {1, 3, 5, 7}. Is 5 ∈ A true?
check.answer: Yes, 5 is one of the elements of A.

screens.title: The whole box U, and counting with n(A)
text: When we work with sets we first say what we are talking about, for example the numbers 1 to 10. This biggest set is called the universal set and is named U.
Every other set in the question is made from elements of U. In a picture, U is a rectangle and each set is a circle inside it. This picture is called a Venn diagram.
n(A) means the number of elements in A. It is a count, not a set.
example: A is the set of even numbers in U.

check.question: B = {3, 6, 9}. What is n(B)?

entries.concept: reading a set written as a rule: {x ∈ U : …}
entries.evidence: The first worked example writes A = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 4} before any lesson explains how to read this notation.

screens.title: A set written as a rule
text: A long set is tiring to list. Instead we can give the rule for joining it, like 'everyone in class 6 who wears glasses'.
{x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 4} is read: 'all x in U such that x is a multiple of 4'.
Here x is just a stand-in name for each element in turn. The colon : means 'such that'. After the colon comes the test.
To list the set, go through U one element at a time and keep the ones that pass the test.
example: U = {1, 2, 3, …, 12}. A = {x ∈ U : x is a multiple of 4}.
Go through U: 4 passes, 8 passes, 12 passes.
No other number in U is a multiple of 4.

entries.concept: the shorthand Σα, Σαβ for sums over the roots
entries.evidence: The worked example writes 'Σα = −1, Σαβ = 5' and 'Σαβ/αβγ' but the sign Σ is never explained.

screens.title: Σ means 'add up all of this kind'
text: α, β and γ (alpha, beta, gamma) are just names for the three roots of a cubic, like x, y and z.
The sign Σ (sigma) is shorthand for 'the sum of all terms like this one'. So Σα means α + β + γ: every root, added.
Σαβ means the sum of every product of two different roots, each pair once: αβ + βγ + γα.
αβγ, with no Σ, is simply the product of all three roots.

check.question: The roots are 1, 1 and 2. What is Σα?

entries.concept: what a derivative is (the slope of a curve at a point), and the notation f′(x), dy/dx, d/dx
entries.evidence: The lesson says 'Differentiable at c means the left and right derivatives at c are equal' and works out '2(1) + a = −3', but this is the first skill to use derivatives and no earlier lesson says what a derivative is or how it is written.

screens.title: How steep is a curve right here?
text: A car's speedometer shows your speed at this very moment, not your average speed for the whole trip. Calculus asks the same question about a graph: how steep is it at this one point?
For a straight line this is easy. Its slope is rise ÷ run, and it is the same everywhere. A curve is different: its steepness changes from point to point.

To find the steepness at a point P, take a second point Q on the curve near P. The straight line through P and Q is called a chord. Work out its slope. Now slide Q closer and closer to P. The chord slopes settle on one number. That number is the slope of the curve at P.
The straight line through P with exactly this slope just touches the curve at P. It is called the tangent at P.
example: The slopes head towards 6. The slope of the curve at x = 3 is 6.

check.question: A straight line rises 6 units for every 2 units across. What is its slope?

screens.title: The derivative, and how we write it
text: The slope of the curve y = f(x) at a point is called the derivative of f at that point. It tells how fast f is changing there: how many units y moves for each unit of x, at that instant.

The slope is different at different x, so the derivative is itself a function. We write it f′(x), read 'f dash of x'. The same thing is also written dy/dx, read 'dee y by dee x'. Think of it as a tiny change in y divided by the tiny change in x that caused it.
Finding the derivative is called differentiating. The symbol d/dx written in front of an expression means 'differentiate this with respect to x'.

A function is differentiable at a point when it has one clear slope there, the same coming from the left as from the right. At a sharp corner the two sides give different slopes, so it is not differentiable there.
example: f(x) = x². Take the chord from x to x + h.
Slope = ((x + h)² − x²) ÷ h = (2xh + h²) ÷ h = 2x + h
As h shrinks towards 0, this heads to 2x.
So f′(x) = 2x, and f′(3) = 6, as we found before.

check.question: For f(x) = x² the derivative is f′(x) = 2x. What is f′(5)?

screens.title: Two slopes to remember
text: A straight line y = mx + c has slope m everywhere. So the derivative of mx + c is just m. The constant c only moves the line up or down. It does not change the steepness, so it gives 0.
The curve y = x² has derivative 2x.
Slopes add. So the derivative of x² + ax + b is 2x + a. These two facts are all this skill needs.

check.question: What is the derivative of 7x + 2?

entries.concept: what a differential equation is and what solving one means
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts 'When dy/dx is a function of x times a function of y, separate the variables' without saying what a differential equation is, that its unknown is a function, or what the starting value is for.

screens.title: An equation about how fast something changes
text: A hot cup of tea cools quickly at first and slowly later: the hotter it is, the faster it cools. Here we know a rule for how fast something changes, and we want to know the thing itself.
An equation that contains a derivative, such as dy/dx = 2x or dy/dx = 3y, is called a differential equation. Its unknown is not a number. It is a whole function y.
Solving it means finding the functions y that fit. Integration brings in a constant C, so there are many of them. Together they are the general solution.
One extra fact, such as 'y = 5 when x = 0', fixes C. It is called the starting value or initial condition. The single function you then get is the particular solution.
example: Given y = 5 when x = 0: 5 = 0 + C, so C = 5
Solution: y = x² + 5. Check: its derivative is 2x.

check.question: Does y = x² + 1 satisfy dy/dx = 2x?
check.answer: Yes, the derivative of x² + 1 is 2x

entries.concept: curves not written as y = f(x): implicit equations and parameters
entries.evidence: The lesson opens with 'defines y implicitly as a function of x' and later 'a curve given in parametric form' without saying what implicit or parametric means.

screens.title: When y is not on its own
text: Most curves so far were written as y = something in x, such as y = x². That is called explicit: y stands alone on one side.
A circle of radius 5 round the origin is x² + y² = 25. Here x and y are mixed together. The equation still ties y to x: choose an x and it tells you which y fit. We say it gives y implicitly.

We can find the slope dy/dx without solving for y first. Differentiate every term with respect to x. Remember that y is a hidden function of x. So, by the chain rule, a term like y² gives 2y × dy/dx, not just 2y. Then solve for dy/dx.

check.question: Is the point (3, 4) on the curve x² + y² = 25?

screens.title: A third letter that drives both
text: Watch an ant walk across a page. At time t seconds it is at x = 2t and y = t². Neither x nor y is given in terms of the other. Both follow the clock.
The extra letter t is called a parameter, and this way of giving a curve is the parametric form. Each value of t gives one point (x, y).
For the slope of the path, compare how fast y and x change with t. In a tiny moment y changes dy/dt times as fast as t, and x changes dx/dt times as fast. So dy/dx = dy/dt ÷ dx/dt.
example: At t = 3 the ant is at (6, 9) and the slope of its path is 3.

check.question: x = 2t and y = t². Where is the point when t = 1?

entries.concept: what an integral is: the sign ∫, dx, antiderivative, + C, limits, area
entries.evidence: The first screen says 'We want ∫ from x = 0 to x = 1 of 2x(x² + 1)² dx' and this skill comes before the other integration skills, so nothing has yet said what ∫, dx, an antiderivative or the limits mean.

screens.title: Running differentiation backwards
text: Differentiating x² gives 2x. Now ask the question backwards: which function has the derivative 2x? One answer is x². Going backwards like this is called integrating, and x² is called an antiderivative of 2x.
We write ∫ 2x dx = x² + C. The tall sign ∫ means 'integrate'. The dx at the end says that the variable is x. The function in between is called the integrand.

Why + C? Because x² + 1 and x² − 7 also have the derivative 2x: a constant has slope 0. C stands for any constant. An integral written like this, with no numbers on the ∫ sign, is called an indefinite integral.
example: Check by differentiating x³ + C: you get 3x² back.

check.question: The derivative of x² is 2x. What is ∫ 2x dx?

screens.title: An integral between two numbers
text: Sometimes the ∫ sign carries two numbers, as in '∫ from 0 to 3 of 2x dx'. They are called the limits of integration: the lower limit and the upper limit. This is a definite integral, and its answer is a number.
To work it out, find an antiderivative F. Then take F(upper limit) − F(lower limit). The constant C cancels in the subtraction, so we leave it out.

What does the number mean? When the graph is above the x-axis, it is the area under the graph y = f(x) between the two limits. Picture the area cut into very thin strips, each of height f(x) and width dx. The sign ∫ is a stretched S for 'sum': add up all the strips.
example: Check with area: under y = 2x from 0 to 3 is a triangle, ½ × 3 × 6 = 9.

check.question: An antiderivative of 2x is x². What is ∫ from 0 to 2 of 2x dx?

entries.concept: what a limit is and the notation lim (x → a)
entries.evidence: The first lesson screen ('0 ⁄ 0 does not mean the limit is 0') already uses 'the limit' and 'lim (x → 3)' before anything says what a limit is or how to read the arrow.

screens.title: Getting closer and closer
text: Walk towards a wall. With each step you cover half of the distance that is left. You never have to touch the wall, but everyone can say where you are heading: the wall.
A limit is the same idea for a function. We ask: as x gets closer and closer to some number a, what number does f(x) head towards? That number is called the limit of f(x) as x approaches a.
We write it lim (x → a) f(x). The arrow → is read 'approaches' or 'tends to'. It means x comes as near to a as we like, from the left and from the right, without having to be equal to a.
A limit is about where f(x) is heading, not about what happens exactly at x = a. So a limit can exist even at a place where the function itself has no value.
example: f(x) = (x² − 1) ÷ (x − 1). At x = 1 this is 0 ÷ 0, which has no value.
The values head towards 2 from both sides.

check.question: As x gets closer and closer to 4, what number does x + 1 get closer to?

entries.concept: the number e and the natural logarithm (log to base e, also written ln)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Limits from the standard limits of sin x/x, (eˣ − 1)/x and log(1 + x)/x' uses e and log, and no lesson anywhere says what the number e is or that log here means the logarithm to base e.

screens.title: A special number called e
text: Put ₹1 in a bank that pays 100% interest a year. If the interest is added once, you end the year with ₹2. If it is added in two halves, 50% and then 50% again, you get 1.5 × 1.5 = ₹2.25. Added every month, you get about ₹2.61. Added every day, about ₹2.71.

Adding the interest more and more often helps, but less and less. The amount does not grow for ever. It settles on one number, about 2.718. This number is called e. Like π, its decimals never end, so it gets a letter of its own.
The function e^x means e raised to the power x. It is the growth function of calculus. e^0 = 1, e^1 is about 2.718 and e^2 is about 7.39.
example: More and more often: closer and closer to 2.718..., which is e.

check.question: Which whole number is e nearest to: 2, 3 or 10?

screens.title: The natural logarithm
text: You met logarithms as the question 'which power?'. The log of 100 to base 10 is 2, because 10² = 100.
The natural logarithm asks the same question with base e: which power of e gives this number? It is written ln x. In calculus, and in these lessons, plain log x means this same base e logarithm.
So ln and e^x undo each other. If you raise e to a power and then take ln, you get the power back: ln(e^x) = x.
example: ln 7.39 is about 2, because e² is about 7.39

check.question: What is ln(e³)?

entries.concept: a function of two variables f(x, y) and its partial derivatives f_x, f_y (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'The total differential and the linear approximation of f(x, y)' uses f(x, y), f_x and f_y before the partial-derivatives skill, and no lesson says what a function of two variables is.

screens.title: A function with two inputs
text: The area of a rectangle depends on two things, its length x and its width y: area = xy. Change either one and the area changes. In the same way, the height of the ground depends on how far east and how far north you stand.
A rule like this is called a function of two variables, written f(x, y). You put in a pair of numbers and get one number out.
Its graph is not a curve. It is a surface, like a hillside drawn over a map: above each point (x, y) of the map, the height is f(x, y).

check.question: f(x, y) = xy. What is f(3, 4)?

screens.title: Changing one input at a time
text: On a hillside, how steep it feels depends on which way you walk. Walk due east, so only x changes, and you feel one slope. Walk due north, so only y changes, and you feel another.

The slope when only x changes is called the partial derivative of f with respect to x. It is written ∂f/∂x, with a curly d, or f_x for short. To find it, treat y as a fixed number and differentiate in x as usual. The partial derivative with respect to y, written ∂f/∂y or f_y, treats x as the fixed number.
For a small step dx in x and dy in y together, the two effects add: f changes by about f_x × dx + f_y × dy.
example: f_y = x² (x treated as a number)

check.question: f(x, y) = 5x + 2y. What is f_x?

entries.concept: second and higher derivatives and the notation f″, f⁽ⁿ⁾, d²y/dx²
entries.evidence: The Maclaurin lesson writes f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) and f″(a) although the skill on second-order derivatives comes later, and nothing before it says what these symbols mean.

screens.title: Differentiating again and again
text: Speed tells how fast your position changes. Acceleration tells how fast your speed changes. So acceleration is a derivative of a derivative.

Differentiate f once and you get f′. Differentiate f′ and you get the second derivative, written f″ ('f double dash') or d²y/dx². It tells how fast the slope itself is changing. Differentiate again for the third derivative, and so on.
Dashes become hard to count, so for the nth derivative we write the number in small brackets: f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) means 'f differentiated n times'. And f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) means: differentiate n times, then put x = 0.
example: Third derivative = 6, and the fourth derivative = 0.

check.question: f(x) = x². What is f″(x)?

entries.concept: what a series for a function is (a function written as an endless polynomial) and where its coefficients come from
entries.evidence: The lesson begins 'A Maclaurin series writes f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) xⁿ/n!' with no word on what it means to write a function as a series or why anyone would.

screens.title: A function as an endless polynomial
text: How does a calculator find e^0.1 or sin 0.1? It cannot look them up. But it is very good at adding and multiplying, and that is all a polynomial needs.

So the idea is to write a hard function as a polynomial that goes on for ever: a + bx + cx² + dx³ + ... Such an endless sum is called a series. The numbers a, b, c, d, ... in front of the powers are its coefficients.

You already know one. The geometric series 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... adds up to 1 ÷ (1 − x) when x is between −1 and 1. So the function 1 ÷ (1 − x) is equal to that series. When x is small, the first few terms already give a very good value.
example: Four terms: 1.111. Each term brings us closer.

check.question: In the series 1 + x + x² + x³ + ..., what is the coefficient of x²?

screens.title: Where the coefficients come from
text: A Maclaurin series is the series of a function in powers of x. Its coefficients come from the derivatives of the function at 0: the coefficient of x to the power n is f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) ÷ n!. Here n! means n × (n − 1) × ... × 2 × 1, so 3! = 6. The sign Σ in the formula only means 'add up all such terms'.

Why does this work? Put x = 0 in the series: only the constant term is left, so it must be f(0). Differentiate once and put x = 0: only the coefficient of x is left, so it is f′(0). Differentiate twice and put x = 0: you get 2 × (coefficient of x²), so that coefficient is f″(0) ÷ 2. Each further step works the same way.
A Taylor series about x = a does the same thing in powers of (x − a), using the derivatives at a instead of at 0. It is the right tool when you care about x near a.
example: f(x) = e^x. Every derivative of e^x is e^x, and e^0 = 1.
So the coefficient of x to the power n is 1 ÷ n!.

check.question: In the Maclaurin series of e^x, what is the coefficient of x²?

entries.concept: the coordinate plane: x-axis, y-axis, origin, and what the two coordinates mean
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'A point (x, y) is x across from the origin, then y up' without saying what the axes, the origin or coordinates are.

screens.title: Two number lines make a map
text: To tell a friend where you sit in class, you might say 'third column, second row'. Two numbers find the place. A coordinate grid does the same for any point on a flat sheet.

Draw a number line lying flat. It is called the x-axis. Draw a second number line standing straight up through its zero. It is called the y-axis. The point where they cross is called the origin. Both lines read 0 there.
On the x-axis, positive numbers are to the right and negative numbers to the left. On the y-axis, positive numbers are up and negative numbers are down.

Every point gets two numbers in brackets, like (4, 3). They are its coordinates. The first, the x-coordinate, says how far across. The second, the y-coordinate, says how far up or down. The order matters: (4, 3) and (3, 4) are different points.
example: To find (4, 3): start at the origin (0, 0).
Then go 3 up. Mark the point.
(3, 4) is 3 right and 4 up: a different point.

check.question: Start at the origin, go 2 to the right and then 5 up. What are the coordinates of the point you reach?

entries.concept: why an equation in x and y can be a circle: x² + y² = r² and (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts from 'x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0' and completes the square; that a circle is the set of points at distance r from the centre, and so has such an equation, is only said seven lessons later.

screens.title: A circle as an equation
text: Tie a goat to a post with a 5 metre rope. With the rope pulled tight it walks in a circle: every point of its path is exactly 5 metres from the post. A circle is all the points at one fixed distance, the radius, from one point, the centre.

Put the centre at the origin. By the distance formula, a point (x, y) is √(x² + y²) away from the origin. So it is on the circle of radius r exactly when x² + y² = r². That is the equation of the circle.

If the centre is (h, k) instead, the same idea gives (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Multiply out the brackets and you get the long 'general' form, with x², y², an x term, a y term and a constant. Completing the square takes you back, so the centre and the radius can be read off.
example: (3, 4): 9 + 16 = 25, so it is on the circle.
(1, 2): 1 + 4 = 5, less than 25, so it is inside.

check.question: What is the radius of the circle x² + y² = 49?

entries.concept: what an ellipse and a hyperbola are, and their parts (foci, centre, vertices, a, b, c, eccentricity)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Eccentricity of an ellipse or a hyperbola' uses e = c/a, foci, semi-axis and c² = a² ∓ b² straight away; no lesson says what an ellipse or a hyperbola is.

screens.title: The ellipse: an oval from two pins
text: Push two pins into a board. Lay a loose loop of string round them, pull it tight with a pencil, and move the pencil all the way round. You draw an oval called an ellipse. The string does not change length, so for every point on the curve, (distance to one pin) + (distance to the other pin) is the same.

Each pin is a focus (plural: foci). The point midway between the foci is the centre. The longest width, through the foci, is the major axis, and half of it is called a. The shortest width is the minor axis, and half of it is b. The ends of the major axis are the vertices. The distance from the centre to a focus is c.
With the centre at the origin and the foci on the x-axis, the equation is x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, and c² = a² − b². The fixed sum of the two distances is 2a.
example: x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, so a = 5 and b = 3.
c² = 25 − 9 = 16, so c = 4. The foci are (4, 0) and (−4, 0).

check.question: For the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, how long is the major axis?

screens.title: The hyperbola: two branches
text: Look at the edge of the light that a table lamp with a round shade throws on the wall. That curve is a hyperbola. It comes from keeping the difference of the two distances to the foci fixed, instead of their sum. The result is two separate branches that open away from each other.

There are still two foci, and a centre midway between them. The two points where the curve crosses the line through the foci are the vertices. The distance from the centre to a vertex is a, and the segment joining the vertices is the transverse axis, of length 2a. The distance from the centre to a focus is c. Now c is bigger than a.
With the centre at the origin and the foci on the x-axis, the equation is x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, and c² = a² + b². The fixed difference of the distances is 2a.
The eccentricity e = c ÷ a says how far a curve is from being a circle. For a circle it is 0, for an ellipse it is between 0 and 1, and for a hyperbola it is more than 1.
example: x²/9 − y²/16 = 1, so a = 3 and b = 4.
c² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = 5. The foci are (5, 0) and (−5, 0).
e = c ÷ a = 5 ÷ 3, which is more than 1.

check.question: An ellipse has a = 5 and c = 4. What is its eccentricity?

entries.concept: the absolute value bars | |
entries.evidence: The area formula 'Area = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + ...|' and the step '½ × |−10| = 5' use the bars, but absolute value is only taught in a class 11 skill.

screens.title: The bars mean size only
text: A lift standing 3 floors below the ground is at floor −3. How far is it from the ground floor? 3 floors. A distance does not care about direction.
The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0 on the number line. It is written with two upright bars: |−3| = 3 and |3| = 3. It removes a minus sign and leaves a positive number as it is.
An area can never be negative. But a formula built from coordinates can come out negative, depending on the order in which you take the points. The bars put that right.

check.question: What is |−7|?

entries.concept: three coordinates (x, y, z) for a point in space, and the z-axis
entries.evidence: The first lesson finds the distance between P(4, −2, 0) and Q(1, −5, −3) 'across the floor (x and y) and then up (z)' without any lesson saying what a third coordinate or the z-axis is.

screens.title: A third number for height
text: A fly is somewhere in your room. Saying '2 metres from this wall and 3 metres from that wall' fixes only a spot on the floor. The fly may be above it. You need a third number: its height.

In space we use three axes that meet at the origin, each at right angles to the other two. Think of a corner of the room: the x-axis and the y-axis run along the floor, and the z-axis runs straight up.

A point is written (x, y, z). To reach it from the origin, go x along the x-axis, then y in the direction of the y-axis, then z straight up (or down if z is negative). Points on the floor have z = 0, so (2, 3, 0) is the floor point directly below (2, 3, 4).
example: To reach (2, 3, 4): go 2 along x, 3 along y, then 4 up.
Distance from the origin, in two steps:

check.question: How high above the floor (the plane z = 0) is the point (5, 1, 7)?

entries.concept: the vector equation of a line r = a + λb (a point plus multiples of a direction), the parameter λ, direction ratios
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Parallel, intersecting or skew lines' gives lines as r⃗ = (…) + λ(…) and the first worked example says 'Direction ratios: B − A', before the form is explained four lessons later; direction ratios are never defined.

screens.title: A line is a start point plus steps
text: To describe a straight road, you can name one place on it and say which way it runs. A line in space is described the same way.

Let a be the position vector of one known point of the line, and let b be a vector that points along the line. Start at a and add any amount of b: r = a + λb. Here λ (the Greek letter lambda) is any number, positive, negative or a fraction. It is called a parameter. Each value of λ gives one point of the line, and every point of the line comes from some λ. A second line usually uses another letter, μ (mu).

The three components of b are called direction ratios of the line. Any multiple of b points along the same line, so (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6) are direction ratios of the same direction. Divide them by the length of b and you get the direction cosines.

check.question: On the line r = (1, 0, 2) + λ(2, 1, −1), which point has λ = 2?

entries.concept: what the equation of a plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 is, and its normal (a, b, c)
entries.evidence: The first lesson measures a distance to 'the plane 2x + 2y − z + 1 = 0' 'along the normal (a, b, c)' before anything says that such an equation is a plane or why (a, b, c) is perpendicular to it.

screens.title: A flat surface and its normal
text: A table top is part of a plane: a flat surface that goes on for ever in every direction. A table leg stands at right angles to it. A direction at right angles to a plane is called its normal.

In space, one equation in x, y and z describes a surface, not a line. The simplest are flat: z = 0 is the floor, and z = 3 is a flat ceiling 3 units up. In general a plane has an equation ax + by + cz + d = 0. A point is on the plane exactly when its coordinates fit the equation.
The numbers in front of x, y and z make a normal vector of the plane: (a, b, c) is at right angles to it. That is why these three numbers appear in the formulas for distances and angles.
example: (1, 1, 2): 4 − 3 = 1, not 0, so it is off the plane.
A step inside the plane, from (3, 0, 0) to (0, 3, 0), is (−3, 3, 0).
Dot it with the normal (1, 1, 1): −3 + 3 + 0 = 0. At right angles.

check.question: Is the point (1, 2, 0) on the plane x + y + z − 3 = 0?

entries.concept: what slope measures (rise ÷ run) and what the equation of a line y = mx + c means
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'A straight line has the same slope everywhere' and uses m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) and y = mx + c, but no lesson says what slope measures or why such an equation is a line.

screens.title: Slope: how steep?
text: A ramp that rises 1 metre for every 2 metres forward is gentle. A ramp that rises 3 metres for every 2 metres forward is steep. We measure steepness by rise ÷ run.

For a line on a grid, pick any two points on it. The rise is the change in y. The run is the change in x. The slope is rise ÷ run, and its letter is m. On a straight line you get the same answer whichever two points you pick. That is what makes it straight.

A line going uphill from left to right has a positive slope. Downhill is negative. A flat line has slope 0. A line going straight up and down has no slope, because its run is 0 and we cannot divide by 0.
example: Slope = 6 ÷ 2 = 3: for every 1 step right, the line goes 3 up.

check.question: A line passes through (0, 0) and (2, 4). What is its slope?

screens.title: An equation that draws a line
text: Take the rule y = 2x + 1. For x = 0, 1, 2 it gives y = 1, 3, 5. Plot (0, 1), (1, 3) and (2, 5): they lie on one straight line.
The equation of a line is a rule that is true for every point on the line and for no other point. To test a point, put its x and y into the equation.

In y = mx + c, the number m is the slope. The number c is where the line crosses the y-axis, because x = 0 gives y = c. It is called the y-intercept. So to write the equation of a line you need two things: its slope, and one point to fix c.
example: From (0, 1) to (1, 3): rise 2, run 1, so the slope is 2. That is m.
It crosses the y-axis at (0, 1), so c = 1.

check.question: What is the slope of the line y = 5x − 2?

entries.concept: what a protractor is and how to place it
entries.evidence: The first lesson begins 'A protractor has two scales running in opposite directions' without saying what a protractor is, where its centre is, or how it is laid on an angle.

screens.title: Meet the protractor
text: A ruler measures length. A protractor measures angles. It is a flat half circle, usually of clear plastic.

Along its curved edge are marks from 0 to 180. Each small step is 1 degree. In the middle of its straight edge is a small mark called the centre. The line through the centre along the straight edge is the zero line.

To measure an angle, put the centre exactly on the corner of the angle. Turn the protractor until the zero line lies along one arm. Then read the number where the other arm crosses the curved edge. There are two rows of numbers so that you can start from the left or from the right. Use the row that shows 0 on your first arm.
example: One arm lies on the 0 of the inner row.
The other arm crosses the mark 60 on the inner row.
The outer row says 120 there. We do not use it, because the outer row does not show 0 on the first arm.

check.question: The first arm is on 0 and the other arm is on 90 of the same row. How big is the angle?

entries.concept: what an angle is, and what a degree (the sign °) means
entries.evidence: The first lesson opens with 'A right angle (90°) is a square corner' before any lesson has said what an angle is or what the sign ° measures.

screens.title: What is an angle?
text: Open a pair of scissors a little. Now open them wide. The two blades start from the same point, and the opening between them changes.
When two straight lines start from one point, the opening between them is called an angle. The angle tells how far one line has turned away from the other.
The size of an angle does not depend on how long the lines are. Long scissors and short scissors opened the same amount make the same angle.
example: Open it a little: a small angle between the covers.
Open it wider: a bigger angle.
Lay it flat: the covers make one straight line.

check.question: Which makes the bigger angle: scissors opened wide, or scissors opened a little?

screens.title: Measuring a turn in degrees
text: We measure length in centimetres. We measure turn in degrees. The sign for degrees is a small raised circle: 90° is read as 90 degrees.
Think of one full turn, all the way round. People agreed to cut it into 360 equal tiny turns. Each tiny turn is 1 degree. So a full turn is 360°.
A half turn is 180°. It makes a straight line. A quarter turn is 90°. It makes a square corner, and it is called a right angle.
example: The corner of a page is a quarter turn, so it is 90°.

check.question: How many degrees is a right angle?

entries.concept: cevian, and the ratio in which a point divides a side
entries.evidence: The lessons multiply 'the three ratios (BD/DC)(CE/EA)(AF/FB)' and speak of 'the cevians' meeting, without saying what a cevian is or what BD/DC measures.

screens.title: Cevians and the parts of a side
text: Tie a string from one corner of a triangular frame to any point on the opposite side. A segment like this, from a corner to a point on the opposite side, is called a cevian (after the mathematician Ceva). Medians, altitudes and angle bisectors are all cevians.
The point D where a cevian from A lands on BC cuts BC into two parts, BD and DC. The ratio BD : DC compares them, and BD/DC is the same ratio written as a fraction.

In the same way, let the cevian from B land at E on CA, and the cevian from C land at F on AB. Go round the triangle one way: B to C, C to A, A to B. That gives three ratios: BD/DC, CE/EA and AF/FB. Ceva's theorem says three cevians pass through one point exactly when these three multiply to 1.
example: Take the three medians: D, E and F are midpoints.
BD = DC, so BD/DC = 1. In the same way CE/EA = 1 and AF/FB = 1.
1 × 1 × 1 = 1, so the three medians meet at one point.

check.question: D is on BC with BD = 2 cm and DC = 6 cm. What is BD : DC in simplest form?

entries.concept: tangent, point of contact and secant
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts 'A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at a right angle' and asks for 'the length of the tangent from P'; what a tangent is appears only in the fourth lesson.

screens.title: A line that just touches
text: Look at a bicycle wheel standing on a flat road. The road touches the wheel at just one point. A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point is called a tangent. That one point is the point of contact.

A line that cuts through a circle meets it at two points; it is called a secant. From a point P outside the circle you can draw two tangents. 'The length of the tangent from P' means the distance from P to the point of contact T.

The spoke that goes straight down to the road is upright. In the same way, the radius drawn to the point of contact always meets the tangent at a right angle. This gives a right-angled triangle to work with.
example: Centre O, radius OT = 3 cm, and P is outside with OP = 5 cm.
Triangle OTP has its right angle at T, so OP is the longest side.

check.question: At how many points does a tangent meet a circle?

entries.concept: the angle an arc makes (subtends) at the centre and on the circle; segment; cyclic quadrilateral
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'An arc makes twice the angle at the centre that it makes at any point on the rest of the circle ... angles in the same segment ... cyclic quadrilateral' with none of these ideas set up (the parts of a circle come three lessons later).

screens.title: The angle an arc makes
text: Sit in a round stadium and look at the two goalposts A and B. The opening between your two lines of sight is an angle. It is the angle that AB makes at your seat.

Take an arc AB of a circle with centre O. Join A and B to O: angle AOB is the angle the arc makes at the centre. Now pick a point C on the rest of the circle and join A and B to C: angle ACB is the angle the arc makes at a point on the circle. Books say the arc 'subtends' these angles; it only means 'makes'.
The key fact of this skill: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle on the same arc.
example: Arc AB makes angle AOB = 100° at the centre.
At a point C on the rest of the circle, angle ACB = 100° ÷ 2 = 50°.
At another such point D, angle ADB = 50° as well.
If AB is a diameter, angle AOB = 180°, so angle ACB = 90°.

check.question: The angle at the centre is 80°. What is the angle at a point on the circle, on the same arc?

screens.title: Segments and cyclic quadrilaterals
text: A chord is a straight line joining two points of a circle. A chord AB cuts the inside of the circle into two pieces. Each piece is called a segment. A diameter cuts it into two equal segments, called semicircles.
'Angles in the same segment' are angles such as ACB and ADB, where C and D are on the circle on the same side of the chord AB. They stand on the same arc, so they are equal.
A quadrilateral with all four corners on one circle is called a cyclic quadrilateral. Points that lie on one circle are called concyclic. In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles add up to 180°.
example: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle A = 70°.
Angle C is opposite angle A.

check.question: Where do the four corners of a cyclic quadrilateral lie?

entries.concept: compasses, centre, radius and arc in a construction
entries.evidence: The first worked construction says 'With centres A and B and radius r > 3 cm, draw arcs' although the skill that explains what compasses do comes after this one.

screens.title: What compasses draw
text: Compasses have two legs: one with a sharp point and one with a pencil. Once you open them, the gap between the point and the pencil stays the same.

Press the point on the paper at a place P and swing the pencil round. You get a circle. If you swing only part of the way, you get a piece of a circle, called an arc. P is the centre. The gap you chose is the radius.
Every point of the arc is the same distance from the centre. So 'with centre A and radius 4 cm, draw an arc' means: open the compasses to 4 cm on a ruler, put the point on A, and draw a curve.
example: Open the compasses to 4 cm. Draw an arc with centre A.
Keep the same opening. Draw an arc with centre B.
The arcs cross at P. P is on both arcs.
So PA = 4 cm and PB = 4 cm: PA = PB.

check.question: An arc is drawn with centre A and radius 5 cm. How far from A is any point on the arc?

entries.concept: bisect, midpoint, perpendicular bisector and angle bisector
entries.evidence: The lesson defines the perpendicular bisector only as 'the set of all points the same distance from A and from B' and never says that to bisect is to cut into two equal parts.

screens.title: Cutting exactly in half
text: Fold a strip of paper so that its two ends meet. The fold cuts the strip into two equal parts. To bisect something means to cut it into two equal parts.
The point that cuts a line segment AB into two equal parts is its midpoint M, so AM = MB. The perpendicular bisector of AB is the line through M that crosses AB at a right angle (90°).
An angle can be bisected too. The angle bisector is the line from the corner of the angle that cuts it into two equal angles.
example: AB = 6 cm. Its midpoint M is 3 cm from A and 3 cm from B.
The line through M at 90° to AB is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
An angle of 80° is bisected into two angles of 40°.

check.question: An angle of 60° is bisected. How big is each part?

entries.concept: congruent triangles, the SSS rule and CPCT
entries.evidence: Step 4 of the worked bisector says 'triangle PAQ ≅ triangle PBQ (SSS)' and the next lesson ends 'by CPCT', but congruence is not taught until class 7.

screens.title: Shapes that fit exactly
text: Put one 10 rupee coin on another. They match exactly: same shape, same size. Two shapes that fit exactly on top of each other are called congruent.
Two triangles are congruent when all three sides and all three angles of one match those of the other. In the lessons, an equals sign with a small wave on top means 'is congruent to'.
The order of the letters tells which corners match. 'Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR' means A lies on P, B on Q and C on R. So AB matches PQ, BC matches QR and CA matches RP.
example: Triangle ABC has AB = 3 cm, BC = 4 cm, CA = 5 cm.
Triangle PQR is congruent to triangle ABC.
PQ matches AB, so PQ = 3 cm.
QR matches BC, so QR = 4 cm. RP matches CA, so RP = 5 cm.

check.question: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR. Which corner of PQR matches B?

screens.title: SSS and CPCT
text: Take three sticks of 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. However you join them, you get the same triangle. So if the three sides of one triangle equal the three sides of another, the triangles are congruent. This rule is called SSS: side, side, side.
Once two triangles are congruent, every matching part is equal, the angles as well. The short name for this is CPCT: corresponding parts of congruent triangles. 'Corresponding' just means matching.
This is how compasses prove things. The arcs give equal sides, SSS gives congruent triangles, and CPCT gives equal angles. In the lessons a double arrow between two statements means 'so'.
example: To bisect an angle at O: an arc with centre O cuts the two arms at P and Q, so OP = OQ (same opening of the compasses).
Arcs with centres P and Q, drawn with one opening, cross at R, so PR = QR. Join OR: it is a side of both triangles OPR and OQR.
Three pairs of equal sides: triangles OPR and OQR are congruent by SSS.
So the matching angles POR and QOR are equal by CPCT. OR cuts the angle in half.

check.question: Two triangles each have sides of 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Are they congruent?

entries.concept: point, line segment and line, and naming them with letters
entries.evidence: The first lesson counts 'line segments' and 'lines' through points A, B, C and writes AB and BA, without saying what a point, a line segment or a line is.

screens.title: Points, line segments and lines
text: Make a dot on paper with a sharp pencil. The dot marks one place. It is called a point. We name a point with a capital letter, such as A.
Make another point B. Join A to B with a ruler. This straight path is a line segment. It has two ends, A and B. We call it AB. Going from B to A is the same path, so BA is the same segment.
A line is also straight, but it does not stop. It goes on and on both ways. We draw a small arrow at each end to show this. A line segment is a piece of a line.
example: Mark three points A, B and C, not in a row.
Join every pair: AB, AC, BC.

check.question: How many end points does a line segment have?

entries.concept: right angle (square corner)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Parallel, perpendicular or neither' says perpendicular lines 'meet at a right angle', but right angles are first taught in class 4.

screens.title: The square corner
text: Look at the corner of your book page. It is a square corner. The corners of a door, a window and a floor tile are square corners too.
A square corner has a special name: a right angle. Two straight lines that meet and make a square corner are called perpendicular.

To test a corner, put the corner of a page into it. If both edges of the page lie along the two lines, it is a right angle. If the lines are closer together or wider apart than the page corner, it is not.
example: The top bar and the stem meet. A page corner fits exactly there.
So the bar and the stem are perpendicular.

check.question: Is the corner of a square tile a right angle?

entries.concept: full turn, half turn and quarter turn
entries.evidence: The lesson on the four directions says 'a quarter turn right' and 'a half turn', but turns and quarters have not been taught by class 2.

screens.title: Full turn, half turn, quarter turn
text: Stand up and face the door. Now turn all the way round, once, until you face the door again. That is one full turn.
Face the door again. Turn until your back is to the door. That is a half turn. You now face the opposite way. Two half turns make one full turn.
A quarter turn is half of a half turn. Turn only until your shoulder points at the door. Four quarter turns make one full turn. A turn to the right goes the way your right hand points.
example: Ravi faces North. He makes a quarter turn right. Now he faces East.
He makes one more quarter turn right. Now he faces South.
Two quarter turns make a half turn, and South is the opposite of North.

check.question: How many quarter turns make one full turn?

entries.concept: names of polygons with 7 to 10 sides, and the base of a solid
entries.evidence: The first worked example asks for the edges of a 'nonagonal pyramid' and another for a 'heptagonal prism'; these names and the word 'base' are never explained.

screens.title: Naming shapes by their sides
text: A flat closed shape with straight sides is called a polygon. Its name tells how many sides it has: triangle 3, quadrilateral 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6, heptagon 7, octagon 8, nonagon 9, decagon 10.
A polygon has as many corners as sides. A corner is also called a vertex. For more than one we say vertices.
A prism or a pyramid is named after its base. The base is the flat face it stands on. A hexagonal prism has a hexagon at the bottom and another at the top. A nonagonal pyramid stands on a nonagon.
example: Take a heptagonal pyramid. Its base is a heptagon, with 7 corners.
It has 1 more corner: the point at the top.

check.question: How many sides does an octagon have?

entries.concept: polyhedron, and what F, V and E stand for
entries.evidence: The lesson states 'For every polyhedron without holes, faces + vertices − edges = 2' without saying what a polyhedron is.

screens.title: What is a polyhedron?
text: Pick up a matchbox and a ball. The matchbox is made only of flat faces. The ball has no flat face at all.
A solid whose faces are all flat polygons is called a polyhedron. Cubes, cuboids, prisms and pyramids are polyhedra. A cylinder, a cone and a sphere are not, because they have curved surfaces.

A face is one flat surface. An edge is the line where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner where edges meet (for more than one we say vertices). In the formula, F is the number of faces, V the number of vertices and E the number of edges.
example: Count on a cube: F = 6 faces.

check.question: Is a cricket ball a polyhedron?

entries.concept: the square of a number and the square root (the signs ² and √)
entries.evidence: The first lesson writes 'c² = a² + b²' and '√5476 = 74' although squares and square roots are a class 8 skill and no lesson here says what ² or √ mean.

screens.title: Squaring a number
text: Lay tiles in a square: 3 rows with 3 tiles in each row. You need 3 × 3 = 9 tiles. A number multiplied by itself is called its square.
We write a small raised 2 for this. 3² is read '3 squared' and means 3 × 3 = 9. In the same way 5² = 5 × 5 = 25 and 10² = 10 × 10 = 100.
Be careful: 5² is not 5 × 2. It is 5 × 5. A square with side 5 cm has an area of 5² = 25 square centimetres, which is why it is called squaring.

check.question: What is 6²?

screens.title: Going back: the square root
text: A square garden has an area of 25 square metres. How long is one side? We need the number that, multiplied by itself, gives 25. That number is 5.
This backwards step is called taking the square root. Its sign is √. So √25 = 5, because 5 × 5 = 25. Also √49 = 7 and √100 = 10.
In a right-angled triangle we add the squares of the two shorter sides, and then take the square root to get the longest side.

check.question: What is √36?

entries.concept: quadrilateral: its corners in order, opposite and neighbouring sides, and the parallel sign
entries.evidence: The first lesson classifies 'quadrilaterals' by 'opposite sides', names them ABCD and writes AB ∥ DC, but no earlier lesson says what a quadrilateral is or how its sides and angles are named.

screens.title: Four-sided shapes and their parts
text: A kite, a door and a tile all have 4 straight sides. Any flat closed shape with 4 straight sides is called a quadrilateral. It has 4 corners and 4 angles.

We name it by its corners in order, going round: ABCD. Its sides are AB, BC, CD and DA. Sides that share a corner are neighbouring sides, like AB and BC. Sides that do not touch are opposite sides, like AB and CD. Angles A and C are opposite angles.
Two sides are parallel when they run in the same direction and would never meet, like railway tracks. In the lessons, two small upright strokes between two names mean 'is parallel to'.
example: AB and DC are opposite sides. They are parallel and equal.
AD and BC are the other pair of opposite sides.
Angle A is opposite angle C.

check.question: In quadrilateral ABCD, which side is opposite to AB?

entries.concept: a letter for an unknown length, and finding it from an equation
entries.evidence: The lesson on unknown sides writes 'AB = (2x + 4) cm, CD = (4x − 2) cm ... 2x + 4 = 4x − 2, so x = 3' with no steps; solving equations is a class 6 skill.

screens.title: A letter that hides a number
text: Sometimes we do not know a length yet. We give it a letter, such as x. The letter stands for a number.
2x means 2 × x. So 2x + 4 means: double the number, then add 4. If x is 3, then 2x + 4 = 2 × 3 + 4 = 10.
4x − 2 means: 4 times the number, then take away 2. If x is 3, then 4x − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10.

check.question: If x = 2, what is 3x?

screens.title: Finding the hidden number
text: Think of a balance. If both pans hold the same weight, it stays level. If you add the same thing to both pans, or take the same thing from both, it still stays level.
Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. If they are 2x + 4 and 4x − 2, then 2x + 4 = 4x − 2. This is called an equation. We want the number x that makes both sides the same.
Do the same thing to both sides until x stands alone. Then put your x back into both sides to check.

check.question: If 3x = 12, what is x?

entries.concept: names of flat shapes (triangle to hexagon)
entries.evidence: The first lesson asks about hexagons and pentagons, but no lesson before it says what these shape names mean (the skill that names triangle, square and circle comes later).

screens.title: Names of flat shapes
text: Look at a page of your book. Run your finger round its edge. The edge has straight parts. Each straight part is called a side.
A flat shape gets its name from how many sides it has. 3 sides: a triangle. 4 sides: a square or a rectangle. 5 sides: a pentagon. 6 sides: a hexagon.
A square has 4 sides that are all the same length. A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides. A circle is round, like a bangle. It has no straight sides at all.
example: A shape has straight sides. Count them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

check.question: A shape has 6 straight sides. What is it called?

entries.concept: names of solid shapes (cube, cuboid, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere)
entries.evidence: The lessons count faces of a cube, a cuboid, a square pyramid, a cylinder, a cone and a sphere before any lesson shows what these solids are.

screens.title: Names of solid shapes
text: A solid shape is a thing you can hold in your hand, like a ball or a box. It is not flat like a drawing.
A cube is like a dice: every face is a square of the same size. A cuboid is like a brick or a matchbox: a box shape. A sphere is like a ball: round all over.

A cylinder is like a tin or a pipe: a circle at each end. A cone is like an ice-cream cone: a circle at one end and a point at the other. A square pyramid has a square at the bottom and 4 triangles that meet at a point on top.
example: It is a box, but its faces are not all the same size.
So it is a cuboid, not a cube.

check.question: Is a ball a cube or a sphere?

entries.concept: regular polygon
entries.evidence: The lesson speaks of 'one regular pentagon (each corner 108°)' and 'a regular polygon' without saying what makes a polygon regular.

screens.title: Regular polygons
text: Look at a square floor tile. All 4 sides are the same length, and all 4 corners are the same angle. A polygon like this is called regular.

A regular polygon has all its sides equal and all its corner angles equal. A triangle with three equal sides is regular, and each of its corners is 60°. A square is regular, and each of its corners is 90°.
A rectangle that is longer than it is wide is not regular. Its corners are all 90°, but its sides are not all equal.
example: Put 4 square tiles round one point.
90° × 4 = 360°: a full turn, so there is no gap.

check.question: A triangle has sides of 3 cm, 3 cm and 5 cm. Is it regular?
check.answer: No, because its sides are not all equal.

entries.concept: coordinates (x, y), the axes, the origin and a line such as x = 5
entries.evidence: The first worked example says 'P is at (0, 5) and the mirror line is x = 5'; x, y, the origin and the x-axis are used with no introduction (the coordinate plane is a class 8 skill).

screens.title: Two numbers find a point
text: In a cinema hall you find your seat with two things: which seat along the row, and which row. On a grid we find a point the same way, with two numbers.
Draw a number line lying flat. It is called the x-axis. Draw another standing up. It is called the y-axis. They cross where both show 0. That crossing point is called the origin, and its letter is O.

Every point gets two numbers in brackets, like (3, 2). The first number is x: how far across from O. The second number is y: how far up from O. The two numbers are called the coordinates of the point.
example: Start at O. Go 3 steps across to the right.
Then go 2 steps up. Mark the point.
(2, 3) is a different point: 2 across, then 3 up.

check.question: For the point (4, 1), how many steps up do you go?

screens.title: A line called x = 5
text: Mark the points (5, 0), (5, 1), (5, 2) and (5, 3). Each one is 5 steps across. They stand one above the other in a straight line going up and down.
That whole line is named x = 5, because every point on it has x equal to 5. In the same way, y = 5 is the line lying flat that is 5 steps up.
To see how far a point is from the line x = 5, compare its x with 5.
example: Is (5, 7) on the line x = 5? Its x is 5, so yes.
5 − 0 = 5, so it is 5 steps to the left of the line x = 5.

check.question: Is the point (5, 2) on the line x = 5?

entries.concept: negative numbers on a number line and on the grid
entries.evidence: The rotation lesson uses the point (−2, 3) and says 'change the sign of both coordinates', but negative numbers are first taught in class 5.

screens.title: Numbers on the other side of zero
text: A lift shows 0 for the ground floor. One floor below the ground it shows −1, and two floors below it shows −2. These are negative numbers.

On a number line, the numbers 1, 2, 3 go to the right of 0. The negative numbers −1, −2, −3 go to the left of 0. The small sign − in front is called the minus sign. −2 is 2 steps to the left of 0, just as 2 is 2 steps to the right.
