text: Some relations say 'these two are alike in some way': has the same birthday month as, has the same remainder as. A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive all at once is called an equivalence relation.
An equivalence relation sorts the set into groups, called equivalence classes. Everything in a group is related to everything in that group (itself included), and nothing is related across groups.
That makes counting easy. In a group of n elements, each of the n is related to each of the n, so the group gives n × n = n² pairs.
example: A = {1, 2, 3}, relation 'both odd or both even'

check.question: An equivalence relation puts 3 elements all in one group. How many ordered pairs does it have?

entries.concept: spread of data, deviation, and the symbols x̄, σ, σ², N
entries.evidence: The first worked example writes 'x̄ = Σfx/N' and 'σ² = Σfx²/N − x̄²' with no lesson saying why spread is measured or what x̄, σ and N stand for.

screens.title: Same mean, different spread
text: Two batters each play 3 matches. Asha scores 49, 50, 51. Bala scores 0, 50, 100. Both have a mean of 50. But Asha is steady and Bala is all over the place. The mean alone cannot show this.
We need a second number that tells how far the values are spread out from the mean. Such a number is called a measure of dispersion (dispersion means spread).
Start with the deviation of each value: value − mean. Asha's deviations are −1, 0, 1. Bala's are −50, 0, 50. Big deviations mean a big spread.
example: Bala's deviations are much bigger: his scores are more spread out.

check.question: All five values in a data set are 7. How far is each value from the mean?

screens.title: Variance σ² and standard deviation σ
text: Some symbols first. N is the number of values. x̄ is read 'x bar' and means the mean. σ is the small Greek letter sigma; it stands for the standard deviation, and σ² for the variance.

Deviations always add up to 0 (the minus ones cancel the plus ones), so we cannot just average them. Instead we square each deviation, which makes it positive, and then take the mean of the squares. That mean is the variance, σ².
Squaring changed the units (runs became 'square runs'), so we take the square root to come back. The square root of the variance is the standard deviation, σ.
A shortcut that gives the same variance: σ² = (the mean of the squares of the values) − x̄².

check.question: The variance of some data is 9. What is the standard deviation?

entries.concept: the symbol Σ, and what Σf and Σfx mean
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Mean of an ungrouped frequency distribution' says 'the total is Σfx and the number of observations is Σf' without ever saying what the symbol Σ means.

screens.title: Σ means 'add them all up'
text: In a frequency table, x is a value and f is its frequency: how many times that value occurs. If the score 3 has f = 2, then 3 was scored twice.
Σ is the Greek capital letter S, called sigma. S for Sum. It is an instruction: add up everything in that column. Σf means 'add all the frequencies'. That gives the number of values.

fx means f × x: the value, counted as many times as it occurs. Σfx means 'work out f × x in each row, then add them all'. That gives the total of all the values. So mean = Σfx ÷ Σf is simply total ÷ how many.

check.question: The frequencies in a table are 3, 4 and 5. What is Σf?

entries.concept: cumulative frequency (a running total)
entries.evidence: The 'Median of grouped data' lesson says 'make a cumulative frequency column' and uses cf in the formula before cumulative frequency is explained (a later lesson in the same skill explains it).

screens.title: Cumulative frequency: counting as you go
text: A shopkeeper counts customers: 3 in the first hour, 5 in the second, 2 in the third. If you ask 'how many so far?', the answers are 3, then 3 + 5 = 8, then 8 + 2 = 10. This running total is the cumulative frequency, written cf.
In a table of marks with classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, the cumulative frequency of a class tells how many students scored less than the upper limit of that class.

It is how we find the middle. With n values, the middle is at position n/2. Go down the cf column: the first class whose cf reaches n/2 holds the median. It is called the median class. The last cf always equals n.
example: So 8 students scored less than 20, and n = 10.
n/2 = 5. The cf first reaches 5 in the class 10–20: that is the median class.

check.question: The frequencies are 4 and 6. What is the cumulative frequency of the second class?

entries.concept: the bars | | (distance, ignoring sign)
entries.evidence: The worked example writes 'the distances |x − x̄| are ...' and the method says 'write each |x − x̄|' without saying what the upright bars mean.

screens.title: The bars | | mean 'how far'
text: Your house is 3 km east of school and your friend's is 3 km west. On a number line you are at 3 and your friend at −3. But both of you are the same distance from school: 3 km.
The bars | | ask only for that distance and drop the sign. |3| = 3 and |−3| = 3. This is called the absolute value. It is never negative.
So |x − x̄| means: how far the value x is from the mean x̄, no matter whether x is above or below it. The mean deviation is the mean of these distances.

check.question: What is |−7|?

entries.concept: what an average (the mean) is
entries.evidence: The lessons 'The mean of data in a frequency table' and 'The median is not the mean ... they are different averages' use the mean and the word average before the mean is introduced (MATH.statistics.averages-intro comes after it).

screens.title: One number for a whole group: the mean
text: Three friends have 2, 4 and 6 sweets. About how many sweets is that for each friend? Put all the sweets in one pile: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12. Now share the pile equally among the 3 friends: each gets 4.
That equal share, 4, is called the mean. Mean = the total of all the values ÷ how many values there are.

An average is one number that stands for a whole set of numbers. The mean is one kind of average. The median (the middle value) and the mode (the most common value) are two other kinds. They can give different answers for the same data.

check.question: What is the mean of 5 and 7?

entries.concept: quartiles and the interquartile range
entries.evidence: The lesson asks to 'estimate the upper quartile (Q3)' and says 'the lower quartile is at n/4' and 'the interquartile range is Q3 − Q1', but never says what a quartile is or what the range tells us.

screens.title: Quartiles cut the data into four equal parts
text: Line up 40 students from the lowest mark to the highest. The median is the mark at the middle of the line: half the students are below it.

Now cut each half in half again. The mark a quarter of the way along the line is the lower quartile, Q1: one quarter of the students are below it. The mark three quarters of the way along is the upper quartile, Q3: three quarters are below it. Quarter, quartile: the same idea.
So with n students, Q1 is at position n/4, the median at n/2 and Q3 at 3n/4. On an ogive you find that position on the upright axis, go across to the curve and read the mark below.
The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1. It is the spread of the middle half of the students. A small value means the middle students have nearly the same marks.
example: Q1 is at position 40 ÷ 4 = 10, the median at 20, Q3 at 30.
Suppose the ogive gives Q1 = 45 marks and Q3 = 65 marks.

check.question: There are 80 students. At which position is the lower quartile Q1?

entries.concept: degrees, and a full turn of 360°
entries.evidence: The sector-angle lesson says 'the whole circle, 360°' and computes 11/20 of 360° in class 4, before measuring angles in degrees is taught (class 5, MATH.geometry.angle-measure).

screens.title: A full turn is 360°
text: Stand up and turn all the way round until you face the same way again. That is one full turn. People long ago cut a full turn into 360 tiny equal turns. Each tiny turn is called one degree, written 1°.
So a full turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180°. A quarter turn, the corner of a book, is 90°.

A slice of a pie chart is called a sector. Its pointed corner sits at the centre of the circle. The size of that corner, in degrees, is the sector's angle. All the slices together go once round the centre, so their angles add up to 360°.
example: A quarter of a class likes mangoes.
Their slice is a quarter of the circle.
The mango sector has an angle of 90°.

check.question: Half the class comes by bus. What is the angle of the bus sector?

entries.concept: line of sight, angle of elevation and angle of depression
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'the angle of elevation (or depression, which is equal to it by alternate angles) links two of its sides' without saying what either angle is.

screens.title: Looking up and looking down
text: Stand on level ground and look straight ahead. Your eyes look along a level line, called the horizontal. Now look up at the top of a tree. The straight line from your eye to the treetop is the line of sight.
The angle of elevation is the angle through which you raise your eyes: the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight, when the object is above you.
Now stand on a balcony and look down at a ball on the ground. The angle through which you lower your eyes from the horizontal is the angle of depression.

In both cases the height, the distance along the ground and the line of sight make a right triangle. The line of sight is its hypotenuse. (We usually ignore the height of the person's eyes unless it is given.)
example: You stand 10 m from a tree. The angle of elevation of its top is 45°.
Opposite = the tree's height h. Adjacent = 10 m.

check.question: From a bridge you look down at a boat. Is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight an angle of elevation or of depression?

entries.concept: what an identity is, and where sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 comes from
entries.evidence: The skill starts by factorising sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 and says 'sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 ... does almost everything', but no lesson says what an identity is or why these are true.

screens.title: An identity is true for every angle
text: An equation like sin θ = 1/2 is true only for some angles. An identity is an equation that is true for every angle you put in. The most important one comes straight from Pythagoras.
In a right triangle, opposite² + adjacent² = hypotenuse². Divide every term by hypotenuse². You get (opposite ÷ hypotenuse)² + (adjacent ÷ hypotenuse)² = 1.
But opposite ÷ hypotenuse is sin θ and adjacent ÷ hypotenuse is cos θ. So sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, whatever the angle θ is.
example: Triangle 3, 4, 5 with θ facing the side 3: sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5

check.question: For some angle, sin²θ = 0.36. What is cos²θ?

screens.title: Two more identities from the same triangle
text: Start again from opposite² + adjacent² = hypotenuse², but this time divide every term by adjacent². You get (opposite ÷ adjacent)² + 1 = (hypotenuse ÷ adjacent)².
opposite ÷ adjacent is tan θ, and hypotenuse ÷ adjacent is sec θ. So tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ, which is the same as sec²θ − tan²θ = 1.
Dividing by opposite² instead gives 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ, the same as cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1. All three identities are Pythagoras' theorem in different clothes.
example: Triangle 3, 4, 5 with θ facing the side 3: tan θ = 3/4, sec θ = 5/4

check.question: If tan²θ = 3, what is sec²θ?

entries.concept: what sin⁻¹ x means, and reading [ , ] and ( , )
entries.evidence: The first lesson asks for 'the domain of sin⁻¹' and lists ranges such as [−π/2, π/2] without saying that sin⁻¹ x is 'the angle whose sine is x' or how the brackets are read.

screens.title: Going backwards: from the ratio to the angle
text: So far you went forwards: give an angle, get a ratio. sin 30° = 1/2. The inverse goes backwards: give the ratio, get the angle. 'Which angle has sine 1/2?' The answer is 30°, or π/6 radians.
This backwards question is written sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6. Read sin⁻¹ x as 'the angle whose sine is x'. In the same way, cos⁻¹ x is the angle whose cosine is x and tan⁻¹ x is the angle whose tangent is x.
Careful: the small −1 here does not mean 'one divided by'. 1 ÷ sin x is cosec x, a different thing.

There is a difficulty. Many angles have the same sine: sin 30° = 1/2 and sin 150° = 1/2. A function must give one answer, so everyone agrees to pick the angle from one fixed stretch of angles. The angle picked is called the principal value.

check.question: sin 90° = 1. What is sin⁻¹(1)?

screens.title: Which numbers go in, which angles come out
text: The domain of a function is the set of numbers you are allowed to put in. The range is the set of answers that come out.
A sine is never more than 1 or less than −1. So 'the angle whose sine is 2' does not exist: you may only put numbers from −1 to 1 into sin⁻¹.

Such a stretch of numbers is written with brackets. [−1, 1] means all numbers from −1 to 1, with both ends included. A round bracket leaves the end out: (0, π) means all numbers between 0 and π, but not 0 or π themselves.
So 'sin⁻¹ has domain [−1, 1] and range [−π/2, π/2]' means: put in any number from −1 to 1, and the answer is an angle from −π/2 to π/2 (from −90° to 90°).
example: sin⁻¹(1/2): 1/2 lies in [−1, 1], so it is allowed. The answer π/6 lies in [−π/2, π/2].
sin⁻¹(2): 2 is outside [−1, 1], so it is not defined.

check.question: Is the number 1 inside the interval (0, 1)?
check.answer: No. The round bracket leaves 1 out.

entries.concept: sin and cos of angles beyond 90° (the unit circle and the four quadrants)
entries.evidence: This skill uses sin(π − θ) = sin θ, negative angles and values like cos⁻¹ in [0, π], and the next skills use 'reference angle and quadrant sign', but sin and cos were only defined for acute angles of a right triangle; the unit-circle definition appears only in a late lesson of MATH.trigonometry.functions, the last skill in the order.

screens.title: Sine and cosine for any angle
text: In a right triangle the angle θ is always between 0° and 90°. So what could sin 150° or cos 180° mean? We need a bigger definition that agrees with the old one.

Draw a circle of radius 1 with its centre at the origin of the x and y axes. This is the unit circle. Start at the point (1, 0) and turn through the angle θ, anticlockwise. You arrive at a point P on the circle.
Definition: cos θ is the x-coordinate of P and sin θ is the y-coordinate of P. And tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ.

For an acute angle this is the old definition: drop a line from P to the x-axis and you get a right triangle with hypotenuse 1, adjacent side x and opposite side y. So cos θ = x ÷ 1 and sin θ = y ÷ 1. But the new definition works for every angle, even negative ones.
example: θ = 90°: P is at the top of the circle, (0, 1). So cos 90° = 0 and sin 90° = 1.

check.question: After a full turn, θ = 360°, the point P is back at (1, 0). What is sin 360°?

screens.title: Four quadrants decide the sign
text: The two axes cut the plane into four quarters, called quadrants. They are numbered I, II, III, IV going anticlockwise, starting at the top right. Angles from 0° to 90° land in quadrant I, 90° to 180° in II, 180° to 270° in III and 270° to 360° in IV.

The signs come from the coordinates of P. In quadrant I, x and y are both positive, so sin and cos are both positive. In II, x is negative and y positive: cos is negative, sin positive. In III both are negative (so tan, their quotient, is positive). In IV, x is positive and y negative: cos positive, sin negative.

The size comes from the reference angle: the acute angle between the line OP and the x-axis (O is the origin, the centre of the circle). P sits at the same height and the same distance sideways as the point for the reference angle, only perhaps on the other side.
example: θ = 150° is in quadrant II. Its reference angle is 180° − 150° = 30°.
For 30°, the point is (√3/2, 1/2). For 150° it is the mirror image: (−√3/2, 1/2).
This also shows sin(180° − θ) = sin θ.

check.question: The angle 100° is in quadrant II. Is cos 100° positive or negative?

entries.concept: an angle as an amount of turning (negative angles, more than 360°)
entries.evidence: The first worked example converts −720° and a later one −695°, but until now angles were corners of triangles between 0° and 180°; no lesson says what a negative angle or an angle beyond a full turn is.

screens.title: Angles that measure turning
text: Think of the hand of a clock, or a wheel. An angle can measure how much something has turned, not just the size of a corner.

Start with a ray pointing to the right. Turn it about its end point. Turning anticlockwise (the opposite way to a clock's hands) is counted as positive. Turning clockwise is counted as negative. So −90° is a quarter turn clockwise.
A turning thing can keep going. One full turn is 360°, two full turns are 720°, and 450° is one full turn and then 90° more. The ray for 450° ends in the same place as the ray for 90°.
So angles can be any number: big, small or negative.
example: 450° = 360° + 90°: one full turn, then a quarter turn.
−90° and 270° end in the same place, pointing straight down.

check.question: A wheel turns −360°. Where does a mark on it end up?
check.answer: Exactly where it started (one full turn clockwise)

entries.concept: what a radian is
entries.evidence: The lesson gives only 'one radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius' before using π radians = 180°; nothing shows what that looks like or why π appears.

screens.title: Measuring an angle with the radius
text: Degrees cut a full turn into 360 parts, a number people chose long ago. There is a more natural way that uses the circle itself.

Draw a circle. Take a piece of string as long as the radius and lay it along the edge of the circle. The curved piece of the edge it covers is an arc. Join the two ends of the arc to the centre. The angle at the centre is 1 radian. It is a little less than 60°.
So the angle in radians tells how many radius-lengths fit along the arc: angle = arc length ÷ radius.
All the way round, the arc is the whole circumference, 2π × radius. That is 2π radius-lengths. So a full turn is 2π radians, which means 2π radians = 360° and π radians = 180°.
example: Radius 5 cm, arc 5 cm: angle = 5 ÷ 5 = 1 radian
Radius 5 cm, arc 10 cm: angle = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 radians
Half the circle: arc = π × 5 cm, so angle = π radians = 180°

check.question: An arc is 3 times as long as the radius. What is the angle at the centre, in radians?

entries.concept: what sin, cos and tan are (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse)
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts with 'the ratios of 30°, 45° and 60°' and evaluates sin 45° sin 30°; no lesson says what sin, cos and tan are or names the sides of a right triangle.

screens.title: Naming the sides of a right triangle
text: Lean a ladder against a wall. The ladder, the wall and the ground make a triangle with a right angle (90°) where the wall meets the ground.
Look at the angle the ladder makes with the ground. Call it θ (a Greek letter, said 'theeta'; it is just a name for an angle).

From the angle θ, each side gets a name. The hypotenuse is the longest side, the one facing the right angle: the ladder. The opposite side is the one across from θ, not touching it: the wall. The adjacent side is the one next to θ that is not the hypotenuse: the ground.
If you look from the other sharp angle (at the top of the ladder), opposite and adjacent swap. The hypotenuse stays the same.
example: A right triangle has sides 3, 4 and 5. The angle θ faces the side 3.

check.question: In a right triangle with sides 5, 12 and 13, which side is the hypotenuse?

screens.title: sin, cos and tan are three divisions
text: Make the ladder triangle bigger or smaller but keep the angle θ the same. Every side grows or shrinks by the same factor (the triangles are similar). So opposite ÷ hypotenuse does not change. That number depends only on the angle θ.

We give three such divisions names. sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse. cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse. tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. They are read 'sine', 'cosine' and 'tangent' of θ, and are called trigonometric ratios.
Why bother? If you know an angle and one side, these ratios give the other sides. That is how people find the height of a tower or a hill without climbing it.
sin 30° = 1/2 means: in every right triangle with a 30° angle, the side opposite that angle is half the hypotenuse.
example: Sides 3, 4, 5 with θ facing the side 3.

check.question: In a right triangle, the side opposite θ is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13. What is sin θ?

entries.concept: cosec, sec and cot, and what sin²θ means
entries.evidence: The lessons ask 'find cot θ', state 'sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ' and evaluate sin²45° before the reciprocal ratios are defined (only in the next skill) and without saying what the small 2 means.

screens.title: Three more ratios, and sin²θ
text: Turn each of sin, cos and tan upside down and you get three more ratios. cosec θ = hypotenuse ÷ opposite = 1 ÷ sin θ. sec θ = hypotenuse ÷ adjacent = 1 ÷ cos θ. cot θ = adjacent ÷ opposite = 1 ÷ tan θ.
They are read 'cosecant', 'secant' and 'cotangent'. A way to remember the pairs: each pair has exactly one 'co': sin with cosec, cos with sec, tan with cot.
One more piece of writing. sin²θ means (sin θ)², that is sin θ × sin θ. The small 2 is put after 'sin' so that nobody thinks the angle is being squared.
example: Sides 3, 4, 5 with θ facing the side 3: sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5, tan θ = 3/4
cosec θ = 5/3, sec θ = 5/4, cot θ = 4/3

check.question: tan θ = 2/7. What is cot θ?

entries.concept: minutes of a degree (46°32′)
entries.evidence: The tables lesson asks for sin 46°32′ and speaks of 'every 6′' without saying that a degree is divided into 60 minutes.

screens.title: Smaller than a degree: minutes
text: One hour is cut into 60 minutes so that we can tell time more exactly. One degree is cut up the same way, for measuring angles more exactly.
1 degree = 60 minutes. A minute of angle is written with a small mark: 60′. So 30′ is half a degree and 6′ is one tenth of a degree.

46°32′ is read '46 degrees 32 minutes'. It is a little more than 46 and a half degrees. Tables list values every 6′ and give a small correction for the 1′ to 5′ in between. For sin and tan the correction is added. For cos it is subtracted, because cos gets smaller as the angle grows.
example: So look in the 46° row under 30′, then use the correction for 2′ (add it for sin and tan, subtract it for cos).

check.question: How many minutes are there in half a degree?

entries.concept: naming a triangle's sides a, b, c opposite the angles A, B, C
entries.evidence: The first lesson is titled 'a/sin A = b/sin B' and its example gives 'A = 30°, B = 45°, a = 2' without saying which side a is.

screens.title: Small letter faces capital letter
text: Until now sin and cos lived in right triangles. The sine rule and cosine rule work in any triangle, so we need a way to name its parts.

Call the corners A, B and C. The same capital letters also stand for the angles at those corners. Each side is named with the small letter of the corner it faces: side a is opposite angle A (it joins B and C), side b is opposite angle B, and side c is opposite angle C.

So a and A never touch: they face each other across the triangle. The bigger an angle, the longer the side facing it. The sine rule says exactly how: a ÷ sin A, b ÷ sin B and c ÷ sin C are all the same number.
example: Triangle ABC with A = 30°, B = 45°, a = 2
a = 2 is the side BC, facing the 30° angle.
b is the side AC, facing the 45° angle. It must be longer than a.
Sine rule: 2 ÷ sin 30° = 2 ÷ 1/2 = 4, so b = 4 × sin 45° = 2√2, about 2.83.

check.question: In triangle ABC, which side is opposite the angle B?
check.answer: Side b (the side joining A and C)

entries.concept: the notation î, ĵ, k̂ and what a position vector is
entries.evidence: The first lesson begins 'Vectors in î, ĵ, k̂ form are added and scaled' and the next uses 'position vectors −6î − k̂' without saying what î, ĵ, k̂ or a position vector is.

screens.title: Three building-block arrows
text: Directions from a street corner sound like '2 blocks east, then 3 blocks north'. You build any trip out of steps in a few fixed directions.

For vectors the fixed steps are î, ĵ and k̂. î is the unit vector along the x-axis, ĵ along the y-axis and k̂ along the z-axis. The hat on top says the length is 1. In components, î = (1, 0, 0), ĵ = (0, 1, 0) and k̂ = (0, 0, 1).
Every vector is so many î plus so many ĵ plus so many k̂. So 2î + 3ĵ − k̂ is the same vector as (2, 3, −1). A missing letter means that component is 0: 4î + 2ĵ = (4, 2, 0).
The position vector of a point P is the arrow from the origin O to P, written OP. Its components are simply the coordinates of P.
example: P is (3, −1, 2). Its position vector is 3î − ĵ + 2k̂.

check.question: Write 5î − 2ĵ + k̂ as components (x, y, z).

entries.concept: what adding vectors and multiplying a vector by a number mean
entries.evidence: The lesson says vectors 'are added and scaled component by component' and asks for 3a − 3b, but never says what the sum of two vectors or a multiple of a vector is as an arrow.

screens.title: Adding arrows, stretching arrows
text: Walk 3 east and 1 north. Then walk 1 east and 2 north. Altogether you have gone 4 east and 3 north. That is vector addition: follow the first arrow, then the second one from where the first ended. The sum is the single arrow from the start to the finish.
This is why vectors are added component by component: the easts add up, and the norths add up.

Multiplying a vector by a number stretches it. 2a is twice as long as a in the same direction. −a has the same length and the opposite direction. Every component is multiplied by the number. The number is called a scalar.
A mixture such as 3a − 2b is called a linear combination of a and b.

check.question: a = (1, 2, 3). What is 2a?

entries.concept: what a vector is: size and direction, components, the vector from A to B, magnitude, unit vector
entries.evidence: The first vectors lesson says direction cosines 'are the components of the unit vector' and works with 'the vector AB' and |AB|, but no earlier lesson says what a vector, a component or a unit vector is.

screens.title: An arrow: how far and which way
text: 'Walk 5 km' does not say where you end up. 'Walk 5 km north-east' does. Some quantities need a direction as well as a size.

A quantity with a size and a direction is called a vector. We draw it as an arrow: its length shows the size and it points in the direction. A movement from one place to another, a velocity and a force are vectors. A quantity with only a size, such as mass or time, is called a scalar.
The vector that takes you from point A to point B is written AB with an arrow on top. Two arrows with the same length and the same direction are the same vector, wherever they are drawn.
example: Walk 3 km east, then 4 km north.
You are now 3 east and 4 north of the start.
Your whole movement is one arrow, 5 km long, from start to finish.

check.question: Is temperature a vector or a scalar?
check.answer: A scalar: it has a size but no direction

screens.title: A vector as three numbers
text: On a grid, a vector is described by how far it goes along each axis. These numbers are its components. The vector (2, 1, 2) goes 2 along x, 1 along y and 2 along z.
To get the vector from A to B, subtract the coordinates of A from those of B: end minus start. In short, AB = B − A.
The length of a vector is called its magnitude and is written with bars, |AB|. By Pythagoras, used twice, it is √(x² + y² + z²), where x, y and z are the components.

check.question: A is (0, 0, 0) and B is (1, 2, 2). What is |AB|?

screens.title: Unit vectors and direction cosines
text: A unit vector is a vector of length exactly 1. It keeps the direction and throws away the size. To make one, divide every component of a vector by its length.

The components of a unit vector have a meaning. Take the angle between the vector and the x-axis. In the right triangle with the vector as hypotenuse, the x-component is the adjacent side. So the cosine of that angle is (x-component) ÷ (length). The same holds for the y-axis and the z-axis.
These three cosines are called the direction cosines, written l, m, n. The undivided components, or any multiple of them, are called direction ratios.

check.question: What is the length of a unit vector?

entries.concept: the two ways to multiply vectors: the dot product gives a number, the cross product gives a vector (right-hand rule)
entries.evidence: The lesson opens with the formulas 'a · b = |a| |b| cos θ, and a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃' and later 'a × b ... (right-hand rule)' without saying what kind of thing each product is, what it measures or what the right-hand rule is.

screens.title: The dot product: one number from two arrows
text: Pull a trolley with a rope held at a slant. Only the part of your pull that points along the floor moves the trolley. The dot product measures this: how much one vector acts along another.

The dot product a · b is a number, not a vector. It equals |a| × |b| × cos θ, where θ is the angle between the two arrows. If they point the same way, cos θ = 1 and the dot product is as big as it can be. If they are at right angles, cos 90° = 0, so the dot product is 0. If the angle is more than 90°, it is negative.
There is an easy way to work it out: multiply the matching components and add. Having two ways to get the same number is what lets us find the angle.

check.question: a = (1, 0, 0) and b = (0, 1, 0). What is a · b?
check.answer: 0, because the two vectors are at right angles

screens.title: The cross product: a new arrow at right angles
text: Turn a screw with a spanner. You push sideways on the handle, yet the screw moves along its own length, at right angles to both the handle and your push. The cross product describes this kind of situation.
The cross product a × b is a vector. It is at right angles to both a and b. Its length is |a| × |b| × sin θ, which is the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b.

There are two opposite directions at right angles to both arrows. The right-hand rule picks one: point the fingers of your right hand along a and curl them towards b. Your thumb shows the direction of a × b. So b × a points the opposite way. The order matters.
example: It points along the z-axis, at right angles to both.
Its length 6 is the area of the 2 by 3 rectangle on a and b.

check.question: Is a × b a number or a vector?

entries.concept: what a parallelepiped is, and why a · (b × c) is its volume
entries.evidence: The first lesson says the size of [a b c] 'is the volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c' and no lesson says what a parallelepiped is.

screens.title: A leaning box
text: Take a neat stack of books and push the top sideways so that the stack leans. Its sides are now slanted parallelograms. A solid whose six faces are all parallelograms is called a parallelepiped. A cuboid is the special case that stands upright.
Such a box is fixed by the three edges that leave one corner. Call them the vectors a, b and c. Its volume is base area × height.

The number a · (b × c) gives exactly this. The length of b × c is the area of the base on b and c, and dotting with a picks out the height. This number is called the scalar triple product and is written [a b c]. It can come out negative, so the volume is its size, |[a b c]|.
If a, b and c all lie flat in one plane, the box has no height and the volume is 0. Such vectors are called coplanar.

check.question: A box has edges 1, 2 and 5 that meet at right angles. What is its volume?
